name: Beetroot
family: Amaranthaceae, the amaranth family (formerly Chenopodiaceae, the goosefoot family)
grown_as: The garden beetroot, a biennial grown as an annual for its round root. William grows a Rainbow mix (AG 10): 'Albina Vereduna' (white), 'Burpee's Golden', 'Chioggia' (ringed red and white) and 'Detroit' (red globe), which is the one drawn.
habit: Year 1: a rosette of upright to spreading leaves 25 to 40 cm high from the top of a swollen round root that sits half out of the soil. Year 2: a leafy, branched, ridged flowering stem 60 to 120 cm high, the branches long, slender and spike-like.

leaf.arrangement: A rosette from the top of the root
leaf.outline: Oval to long heart-shaped, 10 to 20 cm long, the blade often longer than wide
leaf.base: Rounded to slightly heart-shaped or running a little down the stalk
leaf.margin: Entire, no teeth, but wavy and often crinkled
leaf.veins: A broad red midrib with red side veins running out towards the edge, very plain on the green blade
leaf.surface: Smooth, hairless, glossy; often puckered between the veins
leaf.stalk: Fleshy, as long as or longer than the blade, grooved above, deep red to red-purple
leaf.colour: Dark glossy green flushed with red, the veins and stalk red

flower.form: Tiny green flowers with no petals, in small tight clusters spaced along long slender spikes
flower.petals: None: five small green fleshy sepals (perianth segments) curved inwards over the centre
flower.centre: Five stamens, small and yellowish, half hidden
flower.behind: A small leafy bract under each cluster on the lower part of the spike, smaller upwards; the upper clusters have none
flower.carried: In clusters of two to four along long, branching, leafy spikes that make a loose tall plume, the spikes upright to arching
flower.size: Flowers 2 to 3 mm; spikes 20 to 50 cm
flower.season: June to August of the second year

fruit: Each flower cluster ripens into a hard, corky, irregular, knobbly brown lump 3 to 6 mm (the 'seed'), which holds two to four true seeds. These lumps line the dry brown spikes.
seedling: Two strap-shaped to narrow oblong seed leaves 1.5 to 2.5 cm, on a red stem; the first true leaves oval with red stalks. Because each 'seed' holds several seeds, seedlings often come up in small clumps.
winter: Roots lifted before hard frost. A plant left in shrinks to a small rosette on the root top and may rot in wet cold; it flowers the next summer.

leaf: one simple oval leaf, untoothed but wavy
a red stalk and a red midrib with red side veins
glossy and puckered between the veins
bloom: tiny green flowers with no petals in small tight clusters
clusters spaced along a slender spike, a small leaf under each lower cluster only
seed: a corky, knobbly, irregular brown lump, not a smooth seed
seedling: two narrow strap-shaped seed leaves on a red stem
often two or three seedlings from one spot
young: a rosette of oval leaves on red stalks
the red top of the root beginning to swell at the soil
crop: a round deep red-purple root sitting half above the soil
a thin tail root below it
flower: a tall leafy stem with long slender green spikes
flowers in small green clusters, no petals
seedhead: dry brown spikes lined with corky seed clusters

look_alikes: Chard and leaf beet are the same species with thin roots and broader stalks. Mangelwurzel is the same species with a much larger root, often orange, yellow or pink, mostly above ground. Sea beet, the wild form, has a thin woody root and small glossy leaves. Turnip and radish have rough lobed leaves.
